Children and past lives

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
...children who say they have lived before.

Summary:
How could a two-year-old in Louisiana remember being a World War II pilot shot down over the Pacific? Or a boy in Oklahoma recall being a Hollywood extra?

For more than a decade, Prof Jim Tucker has travelled the country meeting families, hearing stories like these, and trying to determine if the children’s memories are valid. Continuing a fifty-year research project at the University of Virginia involving children from all over the world, he decided to focus on cases in the United States, where parents would not expect their children to say such things. The children usually begin talking about a past life at the age of two or three and may talk about a previous family or the way they died in a previous life. Their statements have often been found to be accurate for one particular deceased individual, and some children have recognized members of the previous family. A number have also had birthmarks or defects that matched wounds on the body of the deceased person. We interview Prof Jim Tucker and try to find South African case studies by means of an open call to viewers who have children with stories about past lives.


Further information:
How could a two-year-old in Louisiana remember being a World War II pilot shot down over the Pacific? Or a boy in Oklahoma recall being a Hollywood extra?

For more than a decade, Prof Jim Tucker has travelled the country meeting families, hearing stories like these, and trying to determine if the children’s memories are valid. Continuing a fifty-year research project at the University of Virginia involving children from all over the world, he decided to focus on cases in the United States, where parents would not expect their children to say such things.

The children usually begin talking about a past life at the age of two or three and may talk about a previous family or the way they died in a previous life. Their statements have often been found to be accurate for one particular deceased individual, and some children have recognized members of the previous family. A number have also had birthmarks or defects that matched wounds on the body of the deceased person.

For the last fifty years, doctors at the University of Virginia Division of Perceptual Studies have investigated cases of young children who report memories of previous lives. Dr. Ian Stevenson, the founder of this work, published numerous scholarly articles and books about cases from all over the world. After working with Dr. Stevenson for several years, Dr. Jim Tucker took over the project when Dr. Stevenson retired in 2002. With Life Before Life, he presented an overview of the research. Recently, he has focused on American cases, and he tells of his experiences with some remarkable children in his latest book, Return to Life: Extraordinary Cases of Children Who Remember Past Lives.

JIM B. TUCKER, M.D. is Bonner-Lowry Associate Professor of Psychiatry and Neurobehavioral Sciences at the University of Virginia. He is Director of the UVA Division of Perceptual Studies, where he is continuing the work of Dr. Ian Stevenson with children who report memories of previous lives. A board-certified child psychiatrist, Dr. Tucker worked with Dr. Stevenson for several years before taking over the research upon Dr. Stevenson’s retirement in 2002.

Dr. Tucker was born and raised in North Carolina. He attended the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill, where he graduated Phi Beta Kappa with a BA degree in psychology in 1982, followed by a Medical Degree four years later. He then received training in general psychiatry and child psychiatry at the University of Virginia. After he completed his training, he stayed in Charlottesville and began a successful private practice in psychiatry.

Dr. Tucker, who was raised Southern Baptist, had never seriously considered the idea of reincarnation before reading one of Dr. Stevenson’s book. After learning about the work, he became intrigued both by the children’s reports of past-life memories and by the prospect of studying them using an objective, scientific approach. He contacted the Division and in 1999 began working there half-time. A year later, he gave up his private practice completely to work at the university. He has now published two books and numerous papers in scientific journals. He has spoken before both scientific and general audiences and has made a number of television appearances, including Good Morning America, Larry King Live, and CBS Sunday Morning.

PROPOSAL: We use Prof Tucker as main expert and try to find South African children via an open call for case studies on the Carte Blanche website.

Script:


Jim:
Most of these children recall a violent death. So to hear your child describing a plane crash or being murdered or terrible things happening can be quite difficult for the parents.
V/O:
This is Prof Jim Tucker of the University of Virginia and he is referring to very young children who have vivid memories of dying in a past life.
Jim:
The average age when children start talking about a past life is thirty five months, so they are usually two or three when they start to come out with these things
V/O:
Jim heads up the only university research center in the world that studies children with past life memories in a scientific way. Over a period of 50 years the center has documented over 2500 cases. Some of these - like the case of James Leiniger - are startling.
Jim:
He is a boy in Louisiana with Christian parents who at age two started having horrible nightmares, multiple times a week of a plane crash. He would be kicking his legs up in the air screaming “Airplane crash. On Fire. Little man can’t get out.”
V/O:
James then told his parents he was a pilot who died when he was shot down by the Japanese. He also drew pictures of the crash and said that his plane took off from a ship.
Jim:
And when his parents asked him the name of the boat he said Natoma. Which is a strange name for a US aircraft carrier. But it turned out that there was a USS Natoma Bay that was stationed in the Pacific during World War II. James then aid that he had been shot down over Iwo Jima and that he had a friend there named Jack Larson. Well it tuned out that there was only one pilot of the USS Natoma Bay who was killed in the Iwo Jima operation and this was a fellow named James Huston. Huston’s plane crashed exactly as James had described. James said how the plane got hit in the air, the engine burst into flames and crashed into the water and quickly sank and this is exactly what happened to Huston’s plane. And on the day of the crash the pilot of the pane next to his was Jack Larson.
V/O:
There is no way little James Leiniger could have known all these things …unless he had been there.
Jim:
We have the documentation that was made before James Houston was identified. So it is clear that James said these things and it matched perfectly with this pilot who had died sixty years before.
V/O:
There are a remarkable number of children who, like James, claim past life memories. Ten year old Keira Cowie from Durban, is one of them.
Jackie
And she was playing and she just said “I really miss my snow Mom.” And I said “who is your snow Mom?” and she‘s like “My snow Mom from long ago, when we lived in the snow”.
LINK:
Both Jackie and Keira are convinced that the snow family is Keira’s family from a past life. Keira started talking about this family when she was just a toddler of two and a half years old.
Jackie:
She started talking about that they lived in an ice house and that she used to go and play outside. She mentioned her snow dad but she spoke mostly about her mom, and she started drawing pictures as well.
V/O:
This is one of Keira’s more recent drawings. But the same theme has recurred in her drawings since the age of two and a half years old. The images she depicted were not scenes a toddler raised in Durban would be familiar with – an Inuit or Eskimo family living in a snow-bound land.
Keira:
I remember my Dad was always outside trying to get some fish or some seals, and if did catch anything my mom would go and cook it. But at times there would be polar bears around and my mom would tell me to stay inside
V/O:
Even as a two and a half year old she could recall dogs pulling sleds and a diet of seals and fish - all in remarkable detail. She also said her snow parents looked different and spoke another language.
Jackie:
I just had the impression that it was a long time ago and she said they stayed in like a little village with lots of igloos and the igloos had like windows and they used to put the skins over the windows.
V/O:
Jim’s research has revealed that most of the children describe very recent past lives
Jim:
The average interval between the death of the previous person and the birth of the child is four and a half years but the median interval meaning half are shorter and half are longer is only sixteen months. So it is generally a very recent life, but we have exceptions, we have had cases of fifty years or more.
V/O:
Like James Leiniger, Keira seems to remember a life that was lived a long time ago. Still, her memories of what she called her snow house are very specific.
Keira
When we walked in we would always cover ourselves with a blanket. There was also a stack of blankets for each of us.

Question:
But were they made of material or skins?

Keira:
Skins.
Link:
Jim has also found that in a large number of cases children with past life memories also tend to remember how they died.
Jackie:
I was in the kitchen one day and then she just said “You know Mommy, I remember when I died”. And I said “What do you mean?” And of course then my hair stood up, you know and I said to her “What do you mean?” and she goes “I was playing in the snow.”
Keira:
I was busy playing with my dog and I didn’t see where I was going because obviously I was running around having fun and then I lost my footing and I just fell down a cliff. After that I never remembered anything else. So, I think I must have died then.
LINK:
Another astounding finding in the research is that some people who remember a past life, have physical features in this life which correspond with an injury in a past life.
Jim:
There are a number of cases where the child has a birthmark or even a full birth defect that matches a wound, usually the fatal wound on the body of the previous person. One little girl remembers the life of a man who had his fingers chopped off as he was being murdered and her fingers were grossly deformed.

V/O:
And this little girl remembered having skull surgery before she died. She was born with an inexplicable band along the circumference of her head.

Like James Leiniger many children even recall the names of people from their past lives.

We met Janine Neilsen and her daughter Amber-Leigh in Durban. Janine says when Amber Leigh started to speak about a previous life when she was only three, she mentioned specific names.
Janine:
She discovered that she was a different person and that she had a whole other family where I was not part of it. She became Alex and her mom was Sandy and her father was Johnston and she had two brothers named Jonathan and Tree.
Derek
But these are quite big names for a toddler. I mean Jonathan and Johnston.
Janine
They are very big names and also we did not know anybody with those names, so it was not that she was associating or found… this just came out of nowhere.
V/O:
Today Amber-Leigh has no memories of the past life she once spoke about.
Amber Leigh
I don’t recall any of it. I don’t know where I got that information from. I can’t link it to anything.
V/O:
Jim has written several books on the subject and has found that there are a number of explanations for past life memories.
Jim:
The most obvious interpretation if you are open to it is that they have this knowledge because they remember these things. They are memories of things they experienced in a past life.
V/O:
Other explanations are that it’s pure coincidence….. or that children access the knowledge in a psychic way…. or that parents influence their children.

More recently research in the area of quantum physics has begun to suggest that memories of a past life are scientifically feasible due to the strong link between physical reality and conscious observation.
Jim:
It seems that events on the quantum level don’t really occur until they are observed.
V/O
The implication is that consciousness actually precedes and determines reality rather than the other way round.
Jim:
If you accept the idea that consciousness is fundamental, it’s what the physical reality grows out of, then there is no reason I have to think that our individual consciousnesses are dependent on the physical brain. That after we die and after our brain dies, this fundamental element of consciousness may well be able to continue on. And it looks like in our cases it becomes attached to a new brain and shown up in a new life.
V/O:
Whatever the explanations, Keira’s memories of her previous life with her snow mother are very, very real to her. So real that at times they even eclipse her relationship with Jackie.
Jackie:
I was moaning to her about something and I said to her “You will listen to me because I am your mother.” And she turned and she said “You’re not my mother!”
Derek:
So do you believe in past lives?
Keira:
I do because of what I have experienced. I miss my snow mommy and my snow daddy and the dogs.

Derek:
Still?

Keira:
Just every once in a blue moon.
V/O:
Keira does not recall names or places but in a number of cases names of people from a previous life mentioned by children have enabled Jim and his team to corroborate some of the accounts.
Jim:
We always try to talk with the previous family and look to see how well the child’s statement match with the previous person’s life.
V/O:
This is also what Jim did in the case of James Leiniger and they were indeed able to trace pilot James Huston’s sister.
Jim:
And James and the sister met and they had a good connection. She was convinced that he was her brother returned.

More recently research in the area of quantum physics has begun to suggest that memories of a past life are scientifically feasible due to the strong link between physical reality and conscious observation. Jim: It seems that events on the quantum level don’t really occur until they are observed. V/O The implication is that consciousness actually precedes and determines reality rather than the other way round. Jim: If you accept the idea that consciousness is fundamental, it’s what the physical reality grows out of, then there is no reason I have to think that our individual consciousnesses are dependent on the physical brain. That after we die and after our brain dies, this fundamental element of consciousness may well be able to continue on. And it looks like in our cases it becomes attached to a new brain and shown up in a new life. V/O: Whatever the explanations, Keira’s memories of her previous life with her snow mother are very, very real to her. So real that at times they even eclipse her relationship with Jackie. Jackie: I was moaning to her about something and I said to her “You will listen to me because I am your mother.” And she turned and she said “You’re not my mother!” Derek: So do you believe in past lives? Keira: I do because of what I have experienced. I miss my snow mommy and my snow daddy and the dogs. Derek: Still? Keira: Just every once in a blue moon. V/O: Keira does not recall names or places but in a number of cases names of people from a previous life mentioned by children have enabled Jim and his team to corroborate some of the accounts. Jim: We always try to talk with the previous family and look to see how well the child’s statement match with the previous person’s life. V/O: This is also what Jim did in the case of James Leiniger and they were indeed able to trace pilot James Huston’s sister. Jim: And James and the sister met and they had a good connection. She was convinced that he was her brother returned. metadata.Summary: How could a two-year-old in Louisiana remember being a World War II pilot shot down over the Pacific? Or a boy in Oklahoma recall being a Hollywood extra? For more than a decade, Prof Jim Tucker has travelled the country meeting families, hearing stories like these, and trying to determine if the children’s memories are valid. Continuing a fifty-year research project at the University of Virginia involving children from all over the world, he decided to focus on cases in the United States, where parents would not expect their children to say such things. The children usually begin talking about a past life at the age of two or three and may talk about a previous family or the way they died in a previous life. Their statements have often been found to be accurate for one particular deceased individual, and some children have recognized members of the previous family. A number have also had birthmarks or defects that matched wounds on the body of the deceased person. We interview Prof Jim Tucker and try to find South African case studies by means of an open call to viewers who have children with stories about past lives.
metadata.Further information: How could a two-year-old in Louisiana remember being a World War II pilot shot down over the Pacific? Or a boy in Oklahoma recall being a Hollywood extra? For more than a decade, Prof Jim Tucker has travelled the country meeting families, hearing stories like these, and trying to determine if the children’s memories are valid. Continuing a fifty-year research project at the University of Virginia involving children from all over the world, he decided to focus on cases in the United States, where parents would not expect their children to say such things. The children usually begin talking about a past life at the age of two or three and may talk about a previous family or the way they died in a previous life. Their statements have often been found to be accurate for one particular deceased individual, and some children have recognized members of the previous family. A number have also had birthmarks or defects that matched wounds on the body of the deceased person. For the last fifty years, doctors at the University of Virginia Division of Perceptual Studies have investigated cases of young children who report memories of previous lives. Dr. Ian Stevenson, the founder of this work, published numerous scholarly articles and books about cases from all over the world. After working with Dr. Stevenson for several years, Dr. Jim Tucker took over the project when Dr. Stevenson retired in 2002. With Life Before Life, he presented an overview of the research. Recently, he has focused on American cases, and he tells of his experiences with some remarkable children in his latest book, Return to Life: Extraordinary Cases of Children Who Remember Past Lives. JIM B. TUCKER, M.D. is Bonner-Lowry Associate Professor of Psychiatry and Neurobehavioral Sciences at the University of Virginia. He is Director of the UVA Division of Perceptual Studies, where he is continuing the work of Dr. Ian Stevenson with children who report memories of previous lives. A board-certified child psychiatrist, Dr. Tucker worked with Dr. Stevenson for several years before taking over the research upon Dr. Stevenson’s retirement in 2002. Dr. Tucker was born and raised in North Carolina. He attended the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill, where he graduated Phi Beta Kappa with a BA degree in psychology in 1982, followed by a Medical Degree four years later. He then received training in general psychiatry and child psychiatry at the University of Virginia. After he completed his training, he stayed in Charlottesville and began a successful private practice in psychiatry. Dr. Tucker, who was raised Southern Baptist, had never seriously considered the idea of reincarnation before reading one of Dr. Stevenson’s book. After learning about the work, he became intrigued both by the children’s reports of past-life memories and by the prospect of studying them using an objective, scientific approach. He contacted the Division and in 1999 began working there half-time. A year later, he gave up his private practice completely to work at the university. He has now published two books and numerous papers in scientific journals. He has spoken before both scientific and general audiences and has made a number of television appearances, including Good Morning America, Larry King Live, and CBS Sunday Morning. PROPOSAL: We use Prof Tucker as main expert and try to find South African children via an open call for case studies on the Carte Blanche website.
